newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-MILLION DOLLAR MAN ELKINGTON EYES MASTERS CROWN.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-MILLION DOLLAR MAN ELKINGTON EYES MASTERS CROWN.

text.p: Million dollar man Steve Elkington is riding high and all signs are looking positive for the Australian.
Elkington is the hottest player in the 86-man field that will tee off for the first round of the Masters on Thursday.
"I couldn't be in better position to come and play the Masters 1997," said Elkington who has won a startling $1,006,150 from five events to lead the U.S. tour in earnings.
"I've had a great season so far and I feel relaxed about this week and I feel like my chances are reasonably good as far as playing well."
That sounds like an understatement when one considers the vital signs regarding Elkington.
The late calendar start for this year's Masters has meant that the glorious burst of colour from flowering bushes that usually grace the tournament has come and gone this year.
"It's a shame we don't get to see the blooms this year," said Elkington, who is extremely allergic to pollen. "But it makes things better for me."

Then there is the odd-year edge for Elkington, whose game at Augusta goes cold in even-numbered years. In seven Masters, his stroke average in even years is 74.5 with two missed cuts. His 70.5 average in odd years has produced a third and fifth-place finish.
Family ties also figure in Elkington's favour.

Two years ago, his first child Annie Elizabeth was born in late March 1995. Elkington celebrated with a strong Masters, finishing tied for fifth, and later won his first major, the PGA Championship at Riviera.

Baby son Sam arrived at the end of February this year. One week later, the proud papa promptly collected the $324,000 top prize at the Doral Ryder Open. Three weeks later Elkington won the Players Championship to add a whopping $630,000 to his household bank balance.
"I think it's a good attitude boost," said Elkington about the newest family arrival. "You can draw strength from that."
The biggest Masters factor, of course, is form and Elkington draws great confidence from that.
"I putted real well over the last few weeks," said the 34-year-old Australian, who realises how important that aspect is on the fast-rolling, undulating greens of Augusta National.
Nick Faldo had just one three-putt over 72 holes in winning last year. Ben Crenshaw and Jose Maria Olazabal did not three-putt once in winning the Masters the two previous years.
"But when you're playing well, you're also hitting balls on the fairway and you're hitting good iron shots and your whole game goes to a different level and you don't worry about too many things."
"I have a lot of confidence."
Elkington will play the first round with two-time Masters champion Tom Watson in one of several intriguing pairings.
Defending champion Faldo, trying to become the only player to win back-to-back Masters twice, plays with 21-year-old phenomenon Tiger Woods, the scoring leader on the U.S. tour.

Australian Greg Norman, disappointed runner-up last year, plays alongside young U.S. star Phil Mickelson. Briton Colin Montgomerie and Davis Love form a pairing of star players who have yet to win their first major.
Anticipation is running high, and Elkington, for one, is eager for the bell to ring.
"This tournament has so much hype before you play it," he said. "Even us players sit in the locker room and talk about who do you think's going to do well and so on.
"It's an exciting week for everyone. The world golf scene starts this week."
